The statement is cautiously hawkish: inflation is still elevated, the target range is raised to 4.75–5%, IOER to 4.9%, and balance-sheet runoff continues, while recent banking stress is expected to tighten credit. Literature on the credit channel and the financial accelerator (Bernanke, Gertler, and Gilchrist) implies that bank-driven tightening—rooted in asymmetric information and moral hazard—amplifies the contractionary impact of a given rate hike, pointing to downside risks for activity and hiring beyond the 25 bp move. Narrative and identification work on monetary policy shocks (Romer and Romer; Bernanke and Mihov) supports the view that signaling “some additional firming” amid acknowledged policy lags constitutes a meaningfully restrictive stance aimed at disinflation.

Goodfriend (2002) highlights how paying interest on reserves strengthens the floor system; raising IOER to 4.9% reinforces tight money-market conditions even as liquidity backstops operate. Consistent with Bagehot’s lender-of-last-resort principles and modern standing facilities, the Desk’s repo/RRP settings help contain instability without diluting the restrictive stance. Taken together, this mix suggests a negative skew to growth with a disinflationary tilt to risks (consistent with “inflation-at-risk” perspectives), making the overall tone modestly more negative than a neutral read.
